changes.adapted_text: We construct a smooth divergence-free initial velocity on the three-dimensional torus for which the unforced incompressible Euler equations develop a singularity in finite time. The velocity extends continuously to that time, but the magnitude of its curl at the origin tends to infinity. On compact sets away from the origin the velocity and its first time derivative have limits in every spatial $C^m$ norm. The construction uses a sequence of localized Craik–Criminale waves. The velocity gradient of one wave amplifies the next. At each step we choose an initial velocity correction to cancel the mean error while fixing the final particle positions to first order.

changes.authors_text: We construct smooth periodic initial data for the three-dimensional incompressible Euler equations whose solution blows up in finite time. The velocity remains bounded, while the vorticity magnitude at the origin tends to infinity. Away from the origin, the velocity and its time derivative have smooth spatial limits at the singular time. The construction uses localized Craik–Criminale waves as building blocks of a multi-scale construction.

changes.note: Explains successive wave amplification and distinguishes the localized oscillatory increment from the possibly global mean and Fourier contributions. Gives the continuation criterion in its periodic form.
changes.adapted_text:
At the origin, a wave with small velocity and short wavelength can have a large velocity gradient. We arrange for that gradient to amplify a finer wave. By the time the finer wave has turned far enough to amplify its own successor, its velocity is still small. Repeating the construction over successively shorter intervals produces the finite time $T_*$. The oscillatory part of each addition is supported in a shrinking neighborhood of the origin. The correction to the phase average of the error can extend over the whole torus, as can the effect of the Fourier cutoff. We estimate those terms separately so that the approximate velocities converge to an Euler solution on every compact time interval before $T_*$.

Euler introduced the equations in 1755, a few years after d’Alembert’s work on the vibrating string \[[41](#cite-DAlembert1747), [42](#cite-Euler1757)\]. Lichtenstein and Günther established local existence and uniqueness for sufficiently regular flows in the 1920s \[[43](#cite-Lichtenstein1925), [44](#cite-Gunther1926)\]. For a modern treatment of the initial value problem see Bedrossian and Vicol \[[10](#cite-BedrossianVicol)\]. The Beale–Kato–Majda continuation criterion \[[9](#cite-BKM), p. 62, Theorem and Corollary\], in its periodic form \[[11](#cite-GGPP), Theorem 1\], implies that a smooth solution on $[0,T)$ extends smoothly through $T<\infty$ if $\int_0^T\|\operatorname{curl}u(t)\|_{L^\infty}\,\,\mathrm dt<\infty$.

In a later computation, Hou and Li \[[50](#cite-HouLi2006)\] observed at most double-exponential growth of the maximum vorticity past Kerr’s predicted singular time. Luo and Hou \[[51](#cite-LuoHou2014)\] found numerical evidence for axisymmetric blow-up at the wall of an axially periodic cylinder. For axisymmetric flow without swirl, Childress, Gilbert and Valiant derived a $t^{4/3}$ growth law for the maximum vorticity of an eroding vortex dipole in an asymptotic model and tested the prediction numerically \[[52](#cite-ChildressGilbertValiant2016), Sections 1–2, pp. 1, 4\]. Childress and Gilbert \[[53](#cite-ChildressGilbert2018)\] later proposed a hairpin geometry as an asymptotic model for finite-time blow-up.

changes.note: Places the torus result in relation to lower-regularity whole-space data and smooth data in a cylinder with boundary. Retains the perturbation class in the stability theorem of Elgindi, Ghoul and Masmoudi.
changes.adapted_text:
On $\mathbb R^3$, Elgindi \[[15](#cite-ElgindiSingularity)\] constructed finite-time blow-up from $C^{1,\alpha_0}$ initial data for some $\alpha_0>0$. Elgindi, Ghoul and Masmoudi \[[16](#cite-ElgindiGhoulMasmoudi), Theorems 1 and 2\] obtained stable, locally self-similar blow-up for finite-energy data in this regularity class; the stability in their Theorem 2 is with respect to small axisymmetric perturbations, which may have swirl, in their weighted Sobolev spaces. Chen and Hou \[[28](#cite-ChenHouSmoothI), Theorem 5\] prove nearly self-similar blow-up from smooth axisymmetric data in a periodic cylinder with boundary, using computer-assisted estimates \[[29](#cite-ChenHouSmoothII)\].

Successively finer scales also appear in the constructions of Córdoba and Martínez-Zoroa for the Euler equations with forcing \[[18](#cite-CMZForcedEuler), Section 1.2\] and for forced IPM \[[19](#cite-CMZForcedIPM), Sections 1.2.1–1.2.4\]. Córdoba, Martínez-Zoroa and Zheng \[[17](#cite-CMZUnforcedEuler), Theorem 2\] used a cascade of vorticity layers to obtain blow-up for the unforced Euler equations on $\mathbb R^3$ from $C^{1,\alpha}$ data smooth away from the origin. Related constructions give blow-up with forcing for the inviscid Boussinesq equations \[[20](#cite-CLMZForcedBoussinesq), Theorem 1\], the variable-density Euler equations \[[21](#cite-CLMZNonhomogeneousEuler), Theorem 1\] and the hypodissipative Navier–Stokes equations \[[22](#cite-CMZHypodissipativeNS), Theorem 1\]. Our companion papers proving singularity formation for forced IPM \[[3](#cite-AlpogeBuckmasterCoiculescuIPM), Theorem 2.1\], the forced Boussinesq equations \[[1](#cite-AlpogeBuckmasterBoussinesq), Theorem 1.1\], and the forced Euler equations \[[2](#cite-AlpogeBuckmasterForcedEuler), Theorem 1.1\] use forces smooth in space and time up to the singular time. In the present construction we use Craik–Criminale waves as building blocks and choose the initial velocity at each step so that the limiting solution is unforced.

The normal begins to turn as soon as the wave is launched. The coupling $\eta$ gives it a component towards $-E_2$, which the shear turns towards $E_1$. Measure elapsed time in units of the growth time by putting $\tau=\sqrt{2\sigma\nu}\,t$. As $S\to\infty$ with $\varepsilon$ and the normalized time interval fixed, the components of $k/\lambda$ in the preceding frame tend to $(\tan\varphi,0,1)$, where $$\tan\varphi=\tfrac12\varepsilon\tau^2,\qquad 0\le\varphi<\tfrac\pi2.$$ Thus $\varphi$ is the angle from $E_3$ towards $E_1$ of the limiting normal. changes.adapted_text:
To transfer the affine calculation to the torus, localize the wave near the origin. Give each particle its phase and its cutoff value at time zero, then carry these values by the periodic velocity from the preceding step, called the *parent*. The cutoff vanishes near the faces of a fundamental cell in the particle labels. Hence the wave extends smoothly across opposite faces even when its initial normal has nonintegral components. Transport of phase along a given flow also occurs in the short-wave stability equations of Lifschitz and Hameiri \[[37](#cite-LifschitzHameiri1991), §II, (7), (9), (17)\] and of Friedlander and Vishik \[[38](#cite-FriedlanderVishik1991), (5)–(7)\]. The broader asymptotic-wave theory goes back to Lax \[[39](#cite-Lax1957)\] and Choquet-Bruhat \[[40](#cite-ChoquetBruhat1969), §§2–3, pp. 3–6\]. Velocity gradients now vary from one particle to another, and differentiating the cutoff contributes an error to the Euler equations.

The periodic iteration starts with the stationary shear $U_0(x)=\sin(2\pi x_2)(e_1+\rho e_3)$, where $e_i$ are the coordinate vectors and $\rho>0$ is small. In the initial frame of the first constructed wave, whose normal points along $e_1$ and whose amplitude points along $e_2$, the gradient $\nabla U_0(0)$ has $\nu=2\pi$ and $\eta=2\pi\rho$. Section 6 uses this first wave to start the successive amplifications.
changes.authors_text:
The periodic construction starts from the stationary shear flow $$U_0(x)=\sin(2\pi x_2)(e_1+\rho e_3),$$ where $e_i$ are the coordinate vectors and $\rho>0$ is small. It solves the Euler equations with zero pressure. In the initial coordinate frame its central gradient has $\nu=2\pi$ and $\eta=2\pi\rho$, so that $\varepsilon=\rho$. Its explicit flow supplies the first wave; subsequent waves use the successive gradients they create.

Craik–Criminale waves on $\mathbb R^3$ provide a local model for amplification. For the periodic construction, we localize each wave by a smooth cutoff supported in the interior of a fundamental cell in Lagrangian coordinates. We extend the localized field periodically and transport its phase and cutoff by the preceding periodic velocity, as in geometric optics \[[37](#cite-LifschitzHameiri1991), [38](#cite-FriedlanderVishik1991), [39](#cite-Lax1957), [40](#cite-ChoquetBruhat1969)\]. Since the cutoff vanishes near the cell boundary, the wave vector need not lie in $\mathbb Z^3$. Localization and the spatial variation of the background introduce errors, which the corrections below make small at each step and remove in the limit.

Use the same parent throughout one correction step. It has been smoothed by a Fourier cutoff, so Bernstein’s inequality bounds its higher spatial derivatives by powers of the cutoff frequency. Spatial mollification plays a related role in convex integration \[[6](#cite-BDLSVOnsager), §2.4, Proposition 2.2\]. The Euler residual $R_U$ of this smoothed velocity $U$ includes the effect of discarding its high frequencies.

For the flow $X$ of $U$ from time zero, assign each particle label $a$ in the fundamental cell a phase $k_*\cdot a$, with $k_*\ne0$. Thus $$\theta(t,X(t,a))=k_*\cdot a,\qquad \kappa=\nabla_x\theta.$$ The particle keeps its phase, but the phase surfaces deform and their normal $\kappa$ changes. For a wave after the first, $k_*$ is chosen so that $\kappa=\lambda E_3$ at the origin at launch. To describe the velocity, first keep the phase $s$ independent in a periodic profile $A_1(t,x,s)$ and then put $s=\theta(t,x)$. A spatial derivative of the evaluated profile differentiates both $x$ at fixed $s$ and the phase, with factor $\kappa$. A smooth time cutoff $\widetilde\chi$ switches on each later wave during the first part of its amplification interval. The first wave is present at time zero and uses $\widetilde\chi=1$.

We smoothly truncate the velocity of each step in frequency at the end of the step, to simplify the bookkeeping of derivative estimates, as in the mollification step of convex integration \[[6](#cite-BDLSVOnsager), Section 2.4\]. This introduces a small error, carried to the next step; Subsection 5.7 gives the estimates. Write $U$ for the truncated velocity of the preceding step and $R_U$ for its residual in the Euler equations.

We add the localized wave described in Subsection 1.1, using $F_h$ and a divergence correction. Let $X$ be the flow of $U$ from time zero, and fix a nonzero vector $k_*$. The phase $\theta$ of the localized wave is defined by $$\theta(t,X(t,a))=k_*\cdot a$$ for Lagrangian coordinates $a$ in the fundamental cell. It is the plane phase $k_*\cdot x$ at time zero, transported by $U$. Its gradient $\kappa=\nabla_x\theta$ is the wave vector of the localized wave; for a linear flow, $\theta=\kappa\cdot x$, as in Subsection 1.1. For a wave after the first, $k_*$ is chosen so that $\kappa=\lambda E_3$ at the origin at its activation time, as for the new wave of Subsection 1.1. The leading velocity is $A_1(t,x,\theta(t,x))$. Writing the profile as $A_1(t,x,s)$ with $s$ independent lets us distinguish derivatives of the coefficients from the large term $\kappa\partial_s$ that arises when differentiating through the phase. A wave after the first is multiplied by a cutoff $\widetilde\chi(t)$ in time that vanishes before its amplification interval; for the first wave $\widetilde\chi=1$. The derivative of the cutoff leaves an error of the size of the wave at the start of that interval, also carried to the next step.

changes.adapted_text:
A growing amplitude alone would give only one large gradient. To continue, we must reach a time when its normal and amplitude give the prescribed coupling ratio for the successor. The entries $\nu=E_1\cdot BE_2$ and $\eta=E_3\cdot BE_2$ have distinct effects. The first enters the initial growth rate and the second turns the normal. Their ratio sets the time available for growth.

We first solve the wave equations with these two entries held constant in the preceding wave’s moving frame and pass to the strong-shear limit (Lemma 2.3). We then compare the actual coefficients and amplitudes with this reference system on a prescribed interval. The distinction matters when the amplitude grows exponentially. The comparison must keep errors small *relative* to the growing solution to control the orientation of the amplified wave. The resulting coupling estimates give a crossing and the shear available there (Proposition 2.8).

Of the two entries $
u=E_1\cdot BE_2$ and $\eta=E_3\cdot BE_2$ of the older gradient introduced in Lemma 2.2, the coupling $
u$ helps the preceding shear amplify a new wave, while $\eta$ changes its direction and eventually ends the growth. A small ratio $\eta/
u$ therefore allows a large gain before decay. In the model case of Subsection 1.1 and the limit of an infinitely strong preceding shear, the amplitude of a new wave solves a linear system of two equations with explicit coefficients (Lemma 2.3). Its solution with growing initial data peaks after a large gain (Lemma 2.5), and the wave follows this solution with relative errors that grow only polynomially in the length of the interval (Lemma 2.6). changes.adapted_text:
A localized wave leaves an error in the Euler equations. We add a finite sequence of corrections and truncate the resulting velocity in Fourier space. At the origin the corrected gradient must still contain the shear that amplifies the next wave. We shall recover the rank-one gradient of the leading oscillation there up to an absolute error (5.50). On the whole torus we need two further estimates. The deformation of the new flow must be controlled, and the pressure and the residual must allow another application of the endpoint inverse.

The corrections solve two linear problems over the given parent. The endpoint problem determines a mean on the entire time interval. Its transport of the leading wave enters the equation for the next oscillation, which we solve forward from zero. The expansion leaves a remainder whose frequency power depends on the depth. We keep the error from switching on the wave separate, since it is the growth of the seed after activation that makes this term small.

changes.authors_text:
We correct the localized wave of Section 3 to obtain the parent velocity for the next wave. The corrections must preserve the leading wave’s rank-one contribution to the velocity gradient at the origin, where the next wave is amplified. The new parent must also have controlled flow deformation and satisfy the pressure and residual bound (5.2) for the next endpoint problem.

At each level of the expansion we first remove the phase average of the error using Theorem 4.2. The first mean correction also cancels the residual of the parent. Transport of the leading wave by the new mean then enters the equation for the oscillatory correction. The residual of the new parent has three sources. The depth controls the remainder of the expansion. The wave is small compared with its peak while it is switched on, so its gain controls the error from the time cutoff. The final Fourier cutoff contributes the error estimated in (5.56). Section 7 chooses the parameters to make all three errors small on the scale of the next wave.

Throughout this section the parent is the truncated velocity to which we add the new wave. We prescribe the wave vector and seed at the origin and extend the seed to the labels in the envelope. Section 6 verifies the two assumptions (5.5) on the central pair for the first wave and for each later wave.
